subject: 확증은 어떻게 작동하는가
title: When evidence supports a hypothesis
content: A theory predicts something, the prediction holds, and we count the theory better supported. This reasoning underlies every empirical inquiry, and stating precisely what it amounts to has proved unexpectedly difficult, because the obvious account produces conclusions nobody accepts. On the simplest view, a hypothesis is confirmed by any observation it entails. All ravens are black entails that this raven is black, so a black raven confirms it. Yet the same claim is logically equivalent to saying that anything not black is not a raven, and a green apple confirms that. By the same reasoning a green apple confirms a claim about ravens, which strikes almost everybody as absurd. One response accepts the conclusion and explains away the discomfort. There are vastly more non black things than ravens, so an apple confirms the claim by an amount too small to notice, and our resistance reflects the size of the support rather than its absence. This is coherent and it has never entirely satisfied its critics. A second puzzle concerns which predicate is projected. Observations of green emeralds support the claim that emeralds are green, and they equally support a strange claim that they are green before some future date and blue afterwards. Nothing in the evidence distinguishes the two, so the preference for the ordinary predicate must come from elsewhere, and saying what that source is has generated a large literature. A more promising framework treats confirmation as a matter of probability raised. Evidence supports a hypothesis if it is more likely given that hypothesis than given its denial, which handles many cases well and requires assigning prior probabilities that nobody can justify precisely. The gain in clarity is real and the foundations remain contested.

subject: 함축된 뜻의 책임
title: Answering for what you implied
content: A speaker can create a false impression without stating anything false. Answering a question about somebody's work by saying only that they are always punctual conveys a judgment that the words do not contain, and everybody present understands it. Whether such a speaker has lied is a genuine moral question. The mechanism is well described. Conversation runs on an assumption that participants supply as much relevant information as they can, so an answer that conspicuously withholds something invites the listener to infer why. The inference is drawn by the hearer and yet it was engineered by the speaker, which is exactly what makes responsibility hard to assign. Defenders of a narrow view hold that only assertions can be lies. A speaker who said nothing false made no false claim, and the hearer's inference, however predictable, was their own. This position has the merit of drawing a clear line, and it licenses a technique that anybody can use to deceive while retaining the ability to deny it. The wider view attends to what was done rather than to what was said. If lying is wrong because it deliberately produces a false belief in somebody entitled to the truth, then the method of production is beside the point, and an engineered implication is as culpable as a stated falsehood. Most people's judgments in ordinary cases follow this view. The distinction survives in law and in professional codes, where liability frequently attaches only to statements. That asymmetry is defensible on practical grounds, since implications are harder to prove than assertions, and it should not be mistaken for a moral finding that implying is innocent.

subject: 헌법이 미래를 묶는 일
title: Rules that one generation imposes on the next
content: A constitution restricts what future majorities may decide, and it is difficult to change by design. This means that people long dead constrain people now living, and the arrangement requires justification rather than assumption, since the ordinary democratic argument runs the other way. The objection is straightforward. Those who ratified a document did not consult anybody now alive, circumstances have changed, and a rule that a current majority cannot alter is a rule imposed on them by others. Stated plainly, the arrangement looks like rule by the dead. One defence appeals to what constitutions protect. Certain guarantees — of process, of minority protection, of the conditions under which majorities are formed — are what make democratic decision possible at all, so entrenching them protects self government rather than restricting it. A majority that abolished elections would have used democratic means to end democracy, and preventing that is not undemocratic. A second defence appeals to precommitment. Individuals bind their future selves routinely, arranging matters so that a later moment of weakness cannot undo a considered decision, and a political community can do the same. The analogy is imperfect, since the later self is the same person while a later generation is not. A third position accepts the difficulty and locates the answer in amendability. A constitution that can be changed, with effort, by a sufficiently settled majority is not rule by the dead but a requirement that change be deliberate. On this reading the difficulty of amendment is the whole justification, and constitutions that are effectively unamendable have lost it. Where the threshold should sit is a question of judgment that no principle settles.

subject: 악법도 법인가
title: Whether a wicked statute counts as law
content: A rule may be enacted correctly and command something monstrous. Whether such a rule is law, and what follows for those subject to it, divides two traditions in legal philosophy, and the disagreement is less about words than it first appears. One tradition separates the questions. Whether a rule is law depends on whether it was made by the recognised procedure; whether it should be obeyed is a further moral question. Defenders argue that this separation aids criticism, since calling a wicked rule law while condemning it keeps both facts visible, whereas denying that it is law obscures what actually confronts a citizen and lets officials pretend the problem is technical. The opposing tradition holds that law claims authority, authority generates obligations, and nothing requiring atrocity can generate an obligation, so a sufficiently unjust rule fails at what makes anything law. Courts after major atrocities have reasoned this way when trying officials who complied with the rules of their state, and the reasoning appears in published judgments rather than only in academic argument. Both positions agree on what matters most. Legal validity does not settle moral obligation, obedience is not automatically owed, and an official who applies an unjust rule cannot defend themselves by pointing at where it came from. Two centuries of dispute have established that much. Where they differ is in what to say about the rule itself, and the practical consequence is smaller than the heat of the argument suggests. Somebody accepting that a wicked rule is law may still refuse to apply it and accept the penalty; somebody denying its validity may still be punished. The disagreement concerns how to describe the situation rather than how to act within it.

subject: 모형은 어떻게 설명하는가
title: Learning about the world from something false
content: Scientific models are known to be inaccurate. A model of a population assumes unlimited food, a model of a market assumes perfect information, and nobody believes either. Yet such models are used to explain and predict, and understanding how something false can supply understanding is a genuine problem. One account treats a model as an idealisation. The false assumptions remove factors that are present but unimportant for the question at hand, so the model isolates a mechanism and shows what it would produce alone. On this reading the falsity is deliberate and controlled, and the model explains by showing which factor does the work. A second account treats models as objects in their own right. A modeller constructs a system, studies its behaviour, and then argues that the real system resembles it in relevant respects. The reasoning is by analogy rather than by deduction, which explains why modellers spend so much effort arguing about whether a resemblance holds. Both accounts face the same difficulty. Deciding which factors are unimportant, or which resemblances are relevant, cannot be read off the model, and it depends on background knowledge that the model does not contain. A model can therefore be internally impeccable and useless, which is a familiar experience in several fields. What follows for practice is that a model's assumptions deserve as much attention as its outputs. A result that depends entirely on an assumption known to be false is not a finding about the world, and presenting it as one is among the commoner failures in quantitative work. The honest use states which factors were removed and argues that their removal is safe for the question being asked.

subject: 이론의 미결정성
title: When the evidence cannot choose
content: For any body of evidence, more than one theory can accommodate it. This claim is uncontroversial in a weak form and radical in a strong one, and distinguishing the two is necessary before anything follows from it. The weak version says that evidence never entails a theory, since a theory says more than any finite set of observations, and further observations may overturn it. Nobody disputes this. It establishes that theories are held tentatively rather than proved, which practising scientists say themselves. The strong version claims that for any theory there is a genuine rival, equally supported by all possible evidence, differing in what it says about the world. If true, this would mean that our choice among theories reflects something other than evidence, and the sciences would not be tracking truth in the way they claim. Defenders construct such rivals by adding compensating adjustments — a different account of forces paired with a different account of geometry, producing identical predictions. Critics reply that the constructed rivals are parasitic rather than genuine. They are built by taking a theory and adding complications designed to cancel out, so they have no independent motivation, make no novel predictions, and would never have been proposed by anybody investigating the world. Treating them as equal contenders confuses logical possibility with scientific alternative. A moderate conclusion holds that underdetermination is real, limited, and temporary in most actual cases. Historical episodes where two theories genuinely competed on equal evidential terms were resolved by later evidence rather than by convention, which is what the strong thesis predicts should be impossible. The philosophical claim survives as a caution about certainty rather than as a general defeat of scientific knowledge.

subject: 확률은 무엇에 관한 것인가
title: What a probability is a probability of
content: Saying that a coin has an even chance of landing heads seems clear until somebody asks what the claim describes. Several answers have been defended, they disagree about what probability is, and the disagreement affects how evidence should be handled in practice. One answer identifies probability with frequency. The claim reports what proportion of tosses land heads in a long series, so probability is a fact about collections rather than about individual events. This handles repeatable cases well and struggles elsewhere, since the probability that a particular patient recovers, or that a theory is true, concerns something that happens once and belongs to no natural series. A second answer treats probability as a physical disposition of the setup — a tendency of this coin and this throwing method to produce heads. This applies to single cases, which is the advantage, and it introduces a property that cannot be observed directly and whose relation to observed frequencies must itself be explained. A third answer makes probability a degree of belief. To say the chance is even is to report how confident one is, constrained by rules that prevent incoherent combinations of beliefs. This applies to anything, including scientific hypotheses, and it appears to make probability subjective, which many find unacceptable for claims that seem to describe the world. Practising statisticians divide along roughly these lines, and the division has real consequences. Methods built on frequency treat a hypothesis as either true or false and ask how surprising the data would be; methods built on belief assign probabilities to hypotheses and update them. The two answer different questions, and confusing them produces the widespread misinterpretation of statistical results that professional bodies have repeatedly tried to correct.

subject: 재현은 어떻게 성립하는가
title: What makes a picture a picture of something
content: A portrait represents a person, and explaining how it manages this is harder than it looks. The obvious answer is resemblance, and the obvious answer fails, since resemblance is symmetric while representation is not. A person resembles their portrait exactly as much as the portrait resembles them, and yet the person does not represent the picture. Resemblance is also too common. Any two things resemble each other in some respect, and a picture resembles other pictures far more than it resembles its subject, so resemblance alone cannot pick out what a picture is of. Adding that the resemblance must be sufficient does not help, since caricatures and highly stylised images represent successfully while resembling very little. One influential account replaces resemblance with convention. A picture represents what it does because a practice has established that it does, much as a word means what it means, and learning to read pictures is learning a system rather than exercising natural recognition. This explains stylisation well and struggles with the fact that people recognise depicted objects in traditions they have never encountered. A middle position appeals to seeing in. A viewer looking at a marked surface can see a face in it, which is a genuine perceptual capacity rather than a decoded convention, and representation consists in a surface being designed to support that experience. This accommodates both the recognition and the role of style, since what a viewer can see in a surface depends partly on what they are used to. The intention of the maker completes most accounts. A surface that accidentally resembles somebody does not depict them, which indicates that representation requires somebody meaning it, and no purely perceptual story can supply that.

subject: 형식과 내용의 구분
title: Whether how a work says it can be separated from what it says
content: Criticism routinely distinguishes what a work is about from how it is made. The distinction is useful and it has been attacked repeatedly, on the ground that in the strongest works the two cannot be separated without destroying both. Examining the attack clarifies what criticism can and cannot do. The case for separation is practical. A summary of a novel conveys something, translations preserve something, and adaptations across media carry something over, so there must be a content that survives changes of form. Anybody who has recommended a book has relied on this. The case against points at what those operations lose. A paraphrase of a poem is not the poem, and readers report that what was valuable disappeared in the paraphrase, which suggests the value lay in the particular arrangement rather than in anything extractable. The claim is strongest for poetry and weakest for narrative, which may indicate that the two admit different degrees of separation rather than that the distinction fails outright. A middle position treats form as itself contributing content. A long delayed sentence does not merely present information slowly; the delay is part of what is communicated, and a reader who received the same information immediately would have received something different. On this reading form and content are distinguishable in thought while inseparable in effect, which is enough to save criticism from the objection. What the argument rules out is a certain kind of shortcut. Judging a work by its subject, or praising it for what it is about, treats the content as the whole and misses what the tradition regards as the art. The commonest failure in casual criticism is exactly this, which is why the objection keeps being raised.

subject: 비극을 즐긴다는 것
title: Why anybody chooses to watch suffering
content: People pay to see works that make them grieve, and they report enjoying the experience. Stated plainly this is strange, since the emotions involved are ones anybody would avoid in life, and explaining the attraction has occupied writers on art since antiquity. The oldest account holds that such works arouse pity and fear and then discharge them, leaving the audience relieved. Whether the ancient term meant a purging, a clarification, or something else has been argued for two thousand years, and the explanation has an obvious appeal along with an obvious difficulty: nobody has shown that audiences leave with less pity and fear than they arrived with. A second account locates the pleasure in the art rather than in the emotion. What is enjoyed is the skill of construction, the aptness of the language, and the shape of the whole, and the painful feelings are the price rather than the product. This fits how audiences actually talk about such works, and it does not explain why the painful subject is necessary, since skill could be displayed on pleasant material. A third account attends to the safety. Feeling grief for a fictional person costs nothing that real grief costs, so the emotion can be experienced fully and then set down, which allows a kind of rehearsal that life does not permit. Several writers have argued that this is genuinely valuable rather than merely comfortable. A fourth points at meaning. Suffering in life is arbitrary while suffering in a well made work is placed within a structure that makes it intelligible, and audiences may value the demonstration that such experience can be given a shape at all. This is the account that practitioners most often give of their own work.

subject: 해석에 한계가 있는가
title: Whether any reading of a text is as good as another
content: A work can be read in more than one way, and everybody grants this. Whether every reading is equally allowed is a different question, and the answer decides whether criticism is an argument or just a report of impressions. The open position holds that meaning is made by readers rather than found in texts. A reader brings beliefs, links, and aims, and the text gives marks on a page, so different readers build different works and no outside standard settles it. This position gained ground for good reasons, one being that official readings had often served interests rather than texts. Its difficulty is that it makes disagreement unintelligible. Critics who reject a reading do not act as though they were merely reporting a different response; they argue, quote passages, and expect the other side to give way. If nothing holds reading in check, that whole practice is a mistake, and yet everybody takes part in it, those theorists included. A checked position holds that a text bears some readings and defeats others. It cannot determine one correct reading, and it can render a proposed reading unsupportable by containing what that reading must ignore. On this account reading is like reasoning to the best explanation: several accounts fit, some fit better, and evidence decides between them without ever settling all of it. Overinterpretation supplies a useful test. A reading that needs the text to mean something no order of its words will bear is not a bold reading but a mistake, and readers spot such cases readily even when they cannot state the rule. That shared recognition is evidence that constraints exist even where nobody can specify them fully.

subject: 위작이 왜 문제인가
title: What is wrong with a perfect copy
content: Suppose a forgery is indistinguishable from an original by any examination. Viewers cannot tell them apart, and the aesthetic experience they produce is identical. Explaining what is wrong with the forgery is therefore harder than it appears, since the obvious answers all appeal to something the case has excluded. The economic answer is true and insufficient. Somebody was deceived and lost money, which is a straightforward wrong, and it says nothing about the object. If the forgery were donated openly it would still be regarded as a lesser thing, and that judgment needs explaining. One account appeals to history. A work is not merely a surface but the product of a particular person at a particular moment, and its value includes being that. A copy however exact was made by somebody else later, so it is a different object with a different history, and the aesthetic experience is not the whole of what we value in art. A second account denies that the experiences would remain identical. Knowing that a work is original changes how it is seen, since a viewer attends differently to what they believe to be a first solution rather than a reproduction of one, and this is a psychological claim that has been tested with mixed results. A third account concerns what art is for. If part of the point is that somebody achieved something, then a copy demonstrates only that the achievement can be imitated, which is a considerably smaller accomplishment. The forger's skill is real and it is a different skill. What the case finally shows is that our engagement with art is not purely a matter of what an object looks like, and any theory holding that it is must accept the conclusion that a perfect forgery is as good, which almost nobody does.

subject: 대중 예술의 평가
title: Judging work that was made to sell
content: Popular work is frequently dismissed as commercial and defended as democratic, and both moves substitute a fact about production for a judgment about the work. Sorting out what can properly be said requires separating several claims that usually arrive together. The first claim is that commercial pressure damages quality. This is sometimes true and cannot be assumed, since a great deal of admired art was made to order under commercial pressure, and patronage imposed constraints no less severe than a market does. The relevant question is what a particular constraint does to a particular work, which requires looking rather than inferring. The second claim concerns audience size. Work that reaches many people is sometimes taken to be simpler by necessity, and sometimes taken to be validated by its reach, and neither follows. Reaching an audience requires legibility, which is a genuine constraint, and legibility is compatible with considerable complexity, as several popular traditions demonstrate. A third claim concerns the standards applied. Judging popular work by criteria developed for a different tradition produces predictable verdicts and very little insight, and much dismissal consists of exactly this. Traditions develop their own criteria, and a serious assessment engages with what the form is attempting rather than with what it is not. The opposite error is equally common. Defending work solely because it is popular abandons judgment entirely, and audiences within any popular tradition distinguish sharply between what is good and what is merely successful. Those internal distinctions are where a critic should begin, since the people who care most about a form have usually thought hardest about what makes an instance of it good.

subject: 완곡어법이 감추는 것
title: Words chosen so that nobody pictures anything
content: Certain vocabulary exists to prevent a listener from forming an image. Describing deaths as losses, dismissals as restructuring, or bombing as engagement removes the concrete event and substitutes an abstraction, and the choice is rarely accidental. The moral question is what such substitution accomplishes and who benefits. Some softening is humane. A doctor speaking to a family, or a colleague delivering bad news, may reasonably choose gentler words, and the listener understands perfectly well what is meant. Here the indirection acknowledges difficulty rather than concealing content, and everybody present could state the plain version if asked. Institutional usage frequently works otherwise. Terms are adopted precisely because they prevent the plain version from being pictured, and their use spreads through documents, briefings, and reporting until the plain version sounds inflammatory by comparison. Somebody who describes an event directly then appears biased, which is the mechanism working exactly as intended. Several writers have argued that this is among the most effective political techniques available, since it operates before argument begins. A useful test asks who chose the word. Vocabulary developed by those affected by something tends to be concrete; vocabulary developed by those doing it tends toward abstraction, and comparing the two lists for any contested activity is instructive. The pattern is consistent enough to be diagnostic. What follows is a habit rather than a rule. Translating an abstraction back into what it describes, and noticing whether the translation changes one's response, is a small operation that exposes a great deal. Where the plain version provokes an objection that the abstract version did not, the vocabulary was doing work that nobody argued for.

subject: 행진 음악과 걸음
title: Music written to make people walk together
content: A march exists to coordinate movement. Its tempo must suit a walking pace, its pulse must be unmistakable, and its phrases must be countable by people who are not listening carefully, and every feature of the form follows from those requirements. The tempo range is narrow. Human walking sits within a limited band, and music substantially faster or slower cannot be marched to, so the tradition works within perhaps twenty beats of a standard. Different traditions chose different points in that band, and the difference is audible immediately when two national styles are compared. The emphasis must fall where the foot does. A march places its strongest accent on the beat where the left foot lands, and phrases are built in even counts so that a unit ends where a step ends, which is why marches are almost invariably in groups of two and four. Odd groupings would leave people out of step. Instrumentation follows the requirement to be heard outdoors while moving. Brass and percussion carry in open air, they can be played while walking, and they need no music stand, which is why the tradition developed around exactly those instruments and why string instruments never entered it. The form escaped its function. Composers wrote marches for the concert hall, for funerals, and for the stage, retaining the rhythmic characteristics while abandoning any expectation that anybody would walk. Listeners still respond to the pulse, and several composers have exploited that response by writing marches that turn grotesque, relying on an audience that feels the pull toward walking together and is then made uncomfortable by where the music is going.

subject: 지시문으로 이루어진 작품
title: Art that exists as a set of instructions
content: Some works consist of directions for making something rather than of the thing made. A certificate specifies a wall drawing to be executed by others, a score describes actions to be performed, and the artist may never touch the result. This arrangement raises the question of where the work actually is. The precedent is musical. A composer writes a score and performers realise it, and nobody doubts that the composition is the work while each performance is an instance. Visual artists adopting the model argued explicitly from this analogy, pointing out that music had solved the problem centuries earlier and that painting's attachment to the unique object was a convention rather than a necessity. The consequences are considerable. A work can exist in several places at once, it can be remade after destruction, and its physical realisation can be entrusted to people the artist has never met. Institutions holding such works own instructions and the right to execute them, and installing one means hiring people to make it according to a specification. The instructions vary in tightness. Some specify every dimension and material; others leave decisions to whoever executes, so that each realisation differs and the variation is part of the design. Where the latitude is wide, the question of what counts as a correct execution becomes genuinely difficult, and estates of deceased artists have had to adjudicate it. The approach also carries a claim about what art is. Locating the work in the conception rather than in the object asserts that the thinking is the art and the making is labour, which is a position with a long history and a great many critics. Practitioners have generally been happy to have that argument.

subject: 과학과 사이비의 구획
title: Telling science from what imitates it
content: Some enterprises use the vocabulary of science, cite evidence, and produce publications, while remaining outside it. Stating what distinguishes them has proved considerably harder than the confidence of most people's judgments would suggest, and the failed attempts are instructive. The best known proposal makes falsifiability the criterion. A genuine theory forbids something, so an observation could refute it, whereas a theory compatible with every possible outcome forbids nothing and explains nothing. This captures a real feature and fails as a sharp line, since established theories are routinely defended against contrary evidence by adjusting auxiliary assumptions, and doing so is frequently correct rather than evasive. A second proposal attends to how a field responds over time. A healthy research programme makes novel predictions that are then confirmed, while a degenerating one absorbs anomalies by adding qualifications that predict nothing new. This is more realistic and it can only be applied retrospectively, which limits its usefulness for judging a field now. A third approach abandons a single criterion for a cluster of markers: whether practitioners seek disconfirming evidence, whether results are checked by people who would benefit from overturning them, whether the field revises its claims, and whether it explains away failures by appealing to conspiracy. No single marker is decisive and the pattern is recognisable. What all attempts share is a difficulty with borderline cases. Fields now respected were once dismissed, and fields once respected have been abandoned, so a criterion sharp enough to exclude everything questionable also excludes work that later proved sound. The honest position holds that the boundary is real, that it is fuzzy, and that judging particular cases requires attention to their history rather than the application of a test.

subject: 종이 제작과 지역성
title: Paper made from whatever grew nearby
content: Handmade paper differs from region to region because the fibre available differed. Bark from particular trees, rice straw, hemp, cotton rag, and bamboo each produce a sheet with distinct strength, absorbency, and surface, and the resulting papers shaped what could be written or painted on them. Long fibres make strong thin sheets. Papers made from certain barks can be extremely thin while remaining durable, which suited traditions using them for screens, windows, and conservation repair as well as for writing. Short fibres produce a softer sheet that absorbs readily, which suits an ink applied with a brush and makes correction impossible. The paper therefore selected the technique rather than the reverse. Preparation matters as much as material. Fibres are cooked, beaten, and suspended in water, and the length of beating determines how the sheet forms, so two papers from identical plants can behave quite differently. Some traditions add a mucilage that slows drainage and lets a maker build a very even sheet by rocking the mould, which is a technique with no counterpart elsewhere. Sizing controls absorbency. An unsized sheet drinks ink and spreads it; a sized one holds a line. Traditions using flowing ink wanted one and traditions using fine pen work wanted the other, and papers were made accordingly, which is why writing implements and papers developed together as a system. Machine production standardised most of this. Wood pulp is cheap, abundant, and acidic, so paper made from it degrades within a century, and the durable papers now used for documents intended to last are made by methods closer to the handmade traditions than to the ordinary industrial process.

subject: 지도의 도상과 관습
title: Reading a map is a learned skill
content: A map appears to show what is there, and almost everything about it is a decision. Which features appear, how they are symbolised, what is at the top, and how a curved surface is flattened are all choices, and readers absorb the conventions so early that they experience them as transparent. Selection is the first decision. A map showing everything would be useless, so a cartographer chooses a purpose and includes what serves it, and the same territory yields entirely different maps for a driver, a walker, and a geologist. Nothing on the sheet announces what was left out. Symbolisation carries meaning that is not in the landscape. A road drawn as a thick red line is not red and is not that wide relative to its surroundings, and its prominence reflects an assumption about what the reader wants. Settlements shown as dots of graded size encode a ranking that somebody assigned. Orientation is arbitrary and feels natural. North at the top is a convention of recent centuries; medieval European maps frequently placed east at the top and Islamic maps often placed south there, and both look wrong to modern readers for no reason beyond habit. Projection introduces distortion that cannot be avoided. Flattening a sphere requires sacrificing area, shape, or distance, and every projection chooses which, so a world map necessarily misrepresents something. The projection that became standard in classrooms preserves angles at the cost of enlarging high latitudes enormously, and generations of readers absorbed a badly distorted sense of relative size. Arguments about which projection to teach are therefore arguments about what impression a map should leave, which is a question about purpose rather than about accuracy.

subject: 배우 훈련의 방법들
title: Teaching somebody to be somebody else
content: Acting is taught by several methods that disagree at the root about what an actor should be doing. These disputes are old, they are not settled, and each way produces results one can recognise, which suggests that more than one thing works. One tradition begins from the inside. The actor recalls or builds a feeling, works out what the figure wants at each moment, and lets the behaviour follow, so the playing is grown rather than drawn up. Those who teach it argue that anything else yields a copy of feeling rather than feeling, and audiences catch the difference. A second tradition begins from the outside. The actor builds the figure in the body — how they stand, breathe, and move — and finds that the inner state follows from the outward one. This has a basis in the body and it yields playing that holds up night after night, which the first method famously does not promise. A third emphasises the text. The actor works from what is written, treating rhythm, structure, and word choice as instructions, and this approach dominates where the writing is dense enough to reward it. Its teachers argue that a player who attends closely to the words will reach the figure without any separate inner work. The traditions borrow from each other constantly, and most working actors use elements of all three. What parts them in practice is where a player starts when stuck, and teachers note that students trained in one method alone fail in a way you can predict. The internal method can produce indulgence, the external can produce hollowness, and the textual can produce recitation, which is a reasonable argument for a mixed training.

subject: 표현으로서의 예술
title: Whether art is the expression of feeling
content: One influential account holds that art is the expression of emotion. The artist has a feeling, embodies it in a work, and the audience receives it, so the work is a vehicle carrying an inner state from one person to another. The theory has real appeal and it faces objections that have shaped a century of argument. The first objection concerns the artist. A great deal of admired work was made by people who were not feeling what the work conveys, working to commission, on schedule, and with technical rather than emotional attention. Composers have written cheerful music while miserable, and the theory must either deny this or explain why it does not matter. A refined version answers that the artist expresses an imagined rather than an occurrent feeling, which weakens the account considerably. The second objection concerns the audience. Listeners describe music as sad without feeling sad themselves, so the emotion seems to be attributed to the work rather than transmitted through it. An alternative account holds that works possess expressive properties much as a face possesses them, and recognising sadness in a face requires feeling none. This shifts the question from communication to resemblance. A third position keeps expression while relocating it. What the artist does is not transmit a feeling but articulate one, giving a shape to something that was inchoate before the work existed, and the audience gains access to a formulation rather than to a state. Several artists describe their process in exactly these terms, saying that they discovered what they meant by making it. What survives every version is that expressive vocabulary is indispensable in talking about art. Any theory denying that works are sad, joyful, or serene must explain a practice that nobody is willing to abandon.

subject: 소설이라는 형식의 등장
title: Where the novel came from
content: Long prose stories existed in several traditions well before the eighteenth century, and yet something we would know as the modern novel arose in Europe then and spread fast. Saying what was new means marking this form off from earlier long tales. Earlier prose dealt in types and wonders. Figures stood for kinds, settings were vague or far off, and events tested the hero rather than changing them. What came in the eighteenth century was different: single people, named and dated, in places one could find, whose experience built into change. Critics have called this formal realism, and it is a method rather than a subject. Several conditions supported it. Printing had made books affordable, literacy had spread, and a reading public existed with leisure and money. Lending libraries let readers borrow rather than buy, which made long books pay, and much of the first audience was female, which the content shows. Philosophy supplied a frame. A period preoccupied with individual experience as the source of knowledge produced fiction organised around one person's perception, and the parallel has been drawn frequently enough to be a commonplace. Whether the philosophy caused the form or both responded to the same conditions is unresolved. Its early respectability was low. Novels were held to be trifling and morally shady, defended by their authors in prefaces claiming the story was true, and the habit of offering a novel as a found manuscript or a bundle of real letters comes straight from that unease. Within a century the form had absorbed enough prestige to make such defences unnecessary.

subject: 검열을 피하는 글쓰기
title: Saying it so the censor cannot object
content: Writers working under censorship developed techniques for saying what could not be said, and those techniques left permanent marks on literary form. The methods are consistent across very different regimes, which suggests they are responses to a structural problem rather than local inventions. Displacement is the most common. A story set in a distant country or a remote century can describe present arrangements while denying that it does, and readers who share the situation understand immediately. Censors frequently understood too, which is why historical fiction was banned in several places, and the resulting contest produced increasingly indirect work on one side and increasingly suspicious reading on the other. Allegory works similarly and carries a risk. A sustained parallel can be denied by its author and detected by any attentive reader, and the writer who chooses it accepts that some readers will miss the point entirely. Several major works are read by later audiences without any awareness of what they were addressing. Understatement and omission do work that statement cannot. A passage that describes an ordinary morning and mentions in one clause that a neighbour is no longer there says a great deal to a reader who knows what such absences meant, and nothing that could be quoted in a charge. This produced a prose of extreme restraint in several traditions. The habits outlast the censorship. Writers trained under such conditions frequently continue to work indirectly after the constraint is lifted, and readers continue to read for hidden meaning, sometimes finding it where none was intended. Literary cultures shaped this way retain a characteristic density that scholars can identify long after the political conditions that produced it have gone.

subject: 작가의 의도는 얼마나 중요한가
title: Whether what the maker meant settles anything
content: A work can be interpreted, and the maker had intentions. Whether those intentions determine what the work means is among the most argued questions in criticism, and both extreme positions have been defended vigorously and abandoned by most participants. The strong intentionalist position holds that a work means what its maker meant, so interpretation is the recovery of a mental state and evidence about the maker's beliefs is decisive. This has the merit of making interpretation answerable to something, and it faces the difficulty that intentions are frequently unrecoverable, sometimes multiple, and occasionally unrealised — a writer may have intended an effect that the text does not produce. The opposing position holds that intention is irrelevant. What matters is what the words support, and appealing to the maker's plan is an appeal to something outside the work, which was famously named as a fallacy. This position produced a great deal of close reading and it struggles with cases where knowing the intention plainly changes the reading, such as irony that cannot be detected internally. A middle position distinguishes kinds of intention. What a maker was trying to do — the category, the tradition, the conventions being invoked — is relevant and frequently necessary, since a work read in the wrong genre is misread. What they hoped a reader would feel is less binding, since a work can fail at that while succeeding otherwise. This distinction saves most of what each side wanted. Practical criticism operates roughly this way. Nobody ignores what a maker was attempting, and nobody treats their stated intention as closing the question, and the resulting practice is more defensible than either theory that was argued for.
